v1_text: This issue is particularly relevant to inbred mouse strains, which are genetically diverse despite the continued use of a single C57BL/6J (B6)-based reference genome in most RNA-seq workflows.

v1_text: The Mouse Genomes Project has shown that laboratory mouse strains carry millions of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), short indels, and structural variants relative to the B6 reference assembly \[1,2\].
new_text: The Mouse Genomes Project has shown that laboratory mouse strains carry millions of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), short indels, and structural variants relative to the B6 reference assembly [1,2].

For FVB/NJ the scale of the divergence is substantial: the Mouse Genomes Project calls about 5.0 million homozygous autosomal SNPs and 1.2 million indels relative to GRCm39 in this strain [3], 203,510 of the SNPs within annotated exons, although they are far from uniformly distributed, so that many genes carry no variant at all while others carry tens of SNPs per kilobase.

v1_text: Two main approaches are available to reduce SNP-mediated reference-genome mapping bias.
new_text: Two main approaches are available to reduce SNP-mediated reference-genome mapping bias.

v1_text: The first is WASP, or Variant-Aware Software for Polymorphism, which identifies reads whose alignment changes after allele substitution at variant sites and removes them \[7\].

v1_text: WASP can be applied to standard reference-genome alignments and does not require a personalised reference genome.

v1_text: However, it was developed mainly for allele-specific expression and molecular QTL analyses in heterozygous samples, and its practical effect in pure-strain FVB versus B6 comparisons remains unclear.

v1_text: A second approach is personalised reference alignment, in which strain-specific variant calls are incorporated into the reference sequence before alignment so that the template better matches the strain being analysed.

A read from the B6 haplotype aligns to the B6 reference without mismatches, but its swapped copy carries the FVB alleles of every variant it covers — with 150-bp paired-end reads, often several SNPs in a SNP-dense exon — and fails to remap;

new_text: To test whether the catalog reflects the FVB/NJ reads rather than some property of the loci themselves, we processed 13 mammary tumours from B6.FVB-Tg(MMTV-PyVT)634Mul/LellJ mice (GSE175625), a C57BL/6-congenic line that carries essentially no FVB/NJ alleles (all 13 scored "B6 pure";
mean FVB-allele fraction 0.004–0.018), through the same three arms.

Because this dataset provides no FVB-versus-B6 contrast, we evaluated it with a per-sample reference-swap ratio: log₂ of the FVB-arm count over the naive-arm count for each expressed gene, which is positive when a sample's reads gain from the FVB/NJ reference and negative when they lose.
The genome-wide median of this ratio was 0.000 in every PyVT tumour and in every FVB/NJ and C57BL/6J animal of the four tissues, with 0.3–0.5% of genes at or above +0.5 in every group.
At the catalog genes the three groups separated cleanly in direction (Supplementary Table S3).

FVB/NJ animals gained reads from their own reference (median reference-swap ratio per animal +0.24 to +0.49 over the 138 catalog genes), C57BL/6J animals lost reads (−0.39 to −0.69), and the PyVT tumours also lost reads (−0.08 to −0.16;
77 catalog genes expressed).

Because the C57BL/6J animals of the four tissues contributed to selecting the catalog, we repeated the comparison with the catalog selected from three tissues and evaluated in the held-out fourth tissue;

the held-out C57BL/6J animals again lost reads at those genes (median −0.43 to −0.66 across the four held-out tissues), FVB/NJ animals gained (+0.29 to +0.44), and the PyVT tumours lost (−0.09 to −0.18).
The PyVT tumours thus behave like C57BL/6J animals and unlike FVB/NJ animals at the catalog loci, confirming that the catalog bias is a property of FVB/NJ reads at these loci.
The smaller magnitude of the loss in the PyVT tumours than in C57BL/6J animals was not explained by catalog selection;
possible contributors are discussed below.

The full-site identity scan of the PyVT animals also detected one contiguous block of heterozygous FVB-allele sites on chromosome 16 (37.7–49.7 Mb) in all 13 tumours and in none of 16 C57BL/6J comparison animals, the expected signature of a residual donor-strain segment in a congenic line;

two catalog genes lie in this block (*Cd200r4*, whose PyVT reference-swap ratio was intermediate at −0.26, and *Gm6030*, not expressed in the tumours), and excluding them left the PyVT catalog-gene median unchanged (−0.12).

v1_subsection: Multi-mapping sensitivity analysis reveals two mechanistic classes

new_text: The bias compares a quantification in which both strains are aligned to the FVB/NJ reference with one in which both are aligned to the B6 reference, so it contains two components: the FVB/NJ reads gained when FVB/NJ animals meet their own alleles (bias_matched) and the C57BL/6J reads lost when C57BL/6J animals are aligned to the FVB/NJ sequence (b6_loss;
bias = bias_matched + b6_loss;
Methods).

The two quantities answer different questions: bias_matched changes only the FVB/NJ quantification and so answers whether FVB/NJ expression is underestimated by naive B6 mapping, whereas the bias answers how much the choice of reference changes the strain contrast that an investigator would report.
Genome-wide, both components are centred on zero (median bias_matched −0.0001 and median b6_loss −0.0009 log₂ over all tested gene × tissue pairs).
Applying the fixed catalog criterion to bias_matched alone yields 84 genes, 57 of which are in the primary catalog of 138 (Supplementary Table S3c;
Supplementary Fig. S3).

These 57 genes are supported under both definitions: the personalised reference recovers FVB/NJ reads at them irrespective of what happens to the C57BL/6J reads, and they are the conservative answer to the first question (column `in_matched_reference_catalog` in Supplementary Table S2).

The full set of 84 genes meeting the criterion under bias_matched, which includes 27 genes that do not reach it under the primary definition because the loss of C57BL/6J reads there is negative or small, is described in Supplementary Table S3c.

In the other 81 catalog genes the loss of C57BL/6J reads on the FVB/NJ reference is the larger component — b6_loss exceeds bias_matched in 54 of the 81, and the median share of the bias due to C57BL/6J-read loss is 0.61, against 0.42 in the 57 genes supported under both definitions and 0.50 over the whole catalog.
Of the two worked examples below, *Ndufs5* meets the criterion under both definitions in all four tissues (bias_matched +1.47 to +4.61 log₂;

b6_loss +1.85 to +5.63), whereas *Rps2* meets it under bias_matched in adipose, hypothalamus and liver (+0.73, +1.06, +0.86) but not in skin, where bias_matched is −0.02 and the whole +5.36 log₂ bias is C57BL/6J-read loss (+5.38).
The catalog therefore identifies loci at which the choice of reference changes the strain contrast;

at 57 of them the personalised reference demonstrably recovers FVB/NJ reads, whereas at the others the bias mostly reflects what the FVB/NJ reference does to the C57BL/6J reads, and the FVB/NJ quantification itself is not necessarily corrected.
The catalog is reported unchanged, with both components given per gene (Supplementary Table S2).

To illustrate the practical consequences of SNP-mediated reference-mapping bias, we examine the catalog gene that qualifies most reproducibly and, from the other mechanism class, the gene with the largest single-tissue bias (both chosen by rule;
see Methods).
*Ndufs5* (chromosome 4;

7 FVB/NJ SNPs, 1.27 SNPs/kb) is the most robustly evidenced catalog gene: it exceeded the bias threshold in all four tissues and in both laboratories (adipose +3.85, hypothalamus +3.32, liver +5.14, skin +10.24 log₂;
Fig. 6A).

Under naive alignment, FVB/NJ *Ndufs5* appeared to be expressed at a fraction of the C57BL/6J level (log₂FC −0.92 to −5.06), whereas with the personalised reference it was expressed at a similar or higher level (log₂FC +1.58 to +5.18).

Its multi-mapping sensitivity analysis places it in the SNP-induced multi-mapping class (mean residual fraction 0.24): with multi-mapping reads included, most of the FVB/NJ signal returns to the naive arm, consistent with FVB reads being displaced to related sequences in the B6 reference.

WASP filtering also moved the naive estimate most of the way towards the FVB-arm value in every tissue (bias_wasp +1.55 to +5.52), because the reads it removes are predominantly C57BL/6J reads at the FVB SNP positions.
*Rps2* (ribosomal protein S2;
chromosome 17;

53 FVB/NJ SNPs in a 3.8-kb gene body, 13.9 SNPs/kb) is the catalog gene of the direct-misalignment class with the largest single-tissue bias, and it marks a limit of what a personalised reference can correct with short single-end reads.
In skin, naive alignment reported FVB/NJ *Rps2* at about 1/59 of the C57BL/6J level (log₂FC −5.89);
the FVB arm reported log₂FC −0.53, so the apparent difference disappears (bias +5.36 log₂).
Per-animal expression shows, however, that it disappears not because FVB/NJ reads are recovered (Fig. 6B):

FVB/NJ *Rps2* counts per million were low and essentially the same in every arm (mean log₂(CPM + 1) 2.2 naive, 2.1 WASP, 2.2 FVB reference), whereas C57BL/6J counts fell from 7.7 (naive) to 2.5 (WASP) and 2.6 (FVB reference).
The decomposition says the same: in skin bias_matched is −0.02 log₂ and the entire bias is loss of C57BL/6J reads on the FVB/NJ reference (b6_loss +5.38).

Under unique-only counting the FVB/NJ reads at this locus are not recovered by the SNP-patched reference, and the bias is essentially unchanged by multi-mapping inclusion (residual fraction 0.98 in skin;
0.91–1.04 per tissue).
The reads are not absent: they are multi-mappers on both references.
On the B6 reference they are assigned predominantly to two processed pseudogenes of *Rps2* (fractional counts 49.4 and 44.4 counts per million in FVB/NJ skin against 13.0 at *Rps2*);
on the SNP-patched FVB/NJ reference they are divided almost equally among *Rps2* and the same two pseudogenes (41.8, 37.8 and 32.6);
unique assignment to the pseudogenes is negligible in both strains (repository files `rps2_indels_pseudogenes.md` and `rps2_multimap_cpm.tsv`).
The SNP-patched *Rps2* therefore matches the FVB/NJ reads as well as the pseudogenes do, but not better, so the reads remain multi-mappers and are excluded from unique-only counts.

Because fractional counting raises the FVB/NJ-to-C57BL/6J ratio of *Rps2* by a similar amount on both references (by 1.66 and 1.54 log₂ units), the bias is unchanged when multi-mapping reads are included.
The pseudogenes explain the tie: over the part of the *Rps2* transcript that they copy, *Rps2-ps10* and *Rps2-ps13* carry the FVB/NJ allele at all five exonic SNP positions (*Rps2-ps6* at three;
the other eight exonic SNPs lie in exon segments of other *Rps2* transcripts that the pseudogenes do not contain;
repository file `rps2_pseudogene_alleles.tsv`), so a 52-bp FVB/NJ read from that part matches the pseudogenes as well as it matches *Rps2* on either reference.
The four exonic indels of the FVB/NJ allele all lie outside that part and cannot separate these reads.
The true expression of *Rps2* in FVB/NJ skin is therefore undetermined by this study;
resolving it requires reads that reach positions at which the pseudogenes differ from *Rps2*, or quantification that apportions multi-mapping reads between *Rps2* and its pseudogenes;
a different reference sequence alone would not separate them.
Both worked-example genes lie among the SNP-dense, positively biased loci relative to the genome-wide background (Fig. 6C).
In adipose, hypothalamus and liver, where the reads are longer and paired, *Rps2* qualifies under both bias definitions (bias adipose +1.12, hypothalamus +1.36, liver +1.14, log₂;
bias_matched +0.73, +1.06, +0.86 log₂;
Fig. 6D) and part of the FVB/NJ signal is recovered.

*Rps2* is a highly expressed housekeeping gene, which makes reference-mapping errors at this locus particularly consequential, and it shows that a gene can enter the catalog, and the naive strain difference can vanish under the personalised reference, without the FVB/NJ quantification itself having been corrected.

Finally, to assess whether reference-genome choice affects comparisons made entirely within the FVB/NJ background — the design of most FVB studies — we compared the diet or treatment effect estimated from FVB/NJ animals alone under each arm.

In the three fructose-study tissues no gene was differentially expressed between fructose- and water-fed FVB/NJ mice at FDR < 0.05 under the naive and WASP arms and three genes in liver under the FVB arm, and in skin the imiquimod response was detected with similar power under all three arms (598 genes under naive, 593 under WASP, 539 under the FVB reference, 519 of them shared and concordant in direction between the naive and FVB arms).
Per-gene log₂FC estimates were almost identical between the naive and FVB arms (Pearson r = 0.991–0.997;
0.09–0.38% of genes differed by ≥ 0.5 log₂), and the catalog genes did not deviate (median |Δ log₂FC| 0.02–0.08).
Reference choice therefore changes the absolute level attributed to FVB/NJ alleles at the catalog loci but leaves within-strain contrasts intact.

[8]), and why the field continues to use the B6 reference at all.

The second question is answered empirically by our survey: of 140 FVB RNA-seq studies reporting a reference, all used a B6 assembly, and the practical reasons are evident — the B6 assembly carries the curated Ensembl/GENCODE annotation, the indexes of every aligner, and the coordinate system of every public resource, whereas a strain assembly requires annotation lift-over and loses direct comparability with other datasets.

Our choice follows from the question we set out to answer: we wanted to measure, gene by gene, how much the quantification that investigators actually perform (B6 reference, unique-only counting) departs from a quantification in which FVB/NJ reads meet their own alleles, while keeping the same coordinates, annotation and counting so that the difference can be attributed to the reference sequence alone.
A SNP-patched reference is the minimal intervention that achieves this;

a de novo strain assembly additionally corrects indels, structural variants and assembly gaps and is the better choice when a complete FVB/NJ quantification, rather than a controlled comparison, is the goal. We did not compare the two directly in this study, and that comparison — in particular whether the catalog loci behave the same way against FVB_NJ_v3 — remains to be done.
The B6-congenic PyVT tumours also serve their intended purpose as a negative control.

Their reads behave like C57BL/6J reads at the catalog loci — they lose, rather than gain, counts when swapped onto the FVB/NJ reference, in every comparison including those in which the catalog was selected without the C57BL/6J animals being compared — and unlike FVB/NJ reads, which gain.
This confirms that the catalog describes a property of FVB/NJ reads at these loci rather than of the loci themselves.
The magnitude of the loss in the tumours (median reference-swap ratio −0.08 to −0.16 over the catalog genes) is smaller than in the C57BL/6J animals of the four tissues (−0.39 to −0.69).
Catalog selection does not explain this, as the held-out comparison shows, and the residual chromosome 16 segment contributes only two catalog genes.

A 3′-restricted library would have explained a smaller magnitude, because few reads would then overlap SNPs, but it is not indicated: the GEO record of GSE175625 names no library kit (it records UMI-based read processing), and the fraction of tumour reads overlapping an FVB/NJ SNP (7.7%) lies within the range of the other libraries (4.8–10.8%).

The remaining candidate explanations — the different transcript structure and coverage of a tumour transcriptome, library and read-length differences between the datasets, and the subset of catalog genes expressed in the tumours — cannot be separated with the present data, and we do not interpret the magnitude further.
A methodological lesson of this study concerns the public data themselves.
We verified every sample against the GEO/SRA metadata and, independently, against the FVB-allele fraction in its aligned reads;

the sequence-based check is cheap (minutes per sample on the naive alignment that the pipeline produces anyway) and it is the only step that tests the one assumption on which a strain comparison rests.

In our hands it both confirmed the identity of all 95 animals finally used and rejected a candidate dataset whose four "wild-type C57BL/6J" animals carried fixed non-B6 haplotype blocks on several chromosomes, consistent with an incompletely backcrossed background (GSE55792;
Supplementary Fig. S1);
the same scan at full resolution also revealed a residual heterozygous donor-strain segment on chromosome 16 in every tumour of the B6-congenic PyVT line we used as a negative control.
Neither observation is visible in the metadata, and neither is a criticism of the studies concerned, whose designs did not depend on the point;

but for any analysis that depends on the strain of publicly deposited samples we recommend treating a sequence-based identity check as a mandatory quality-control step and reporting its results, as we do in Supplementary Table S1.

Reference-genome choice could in principle also affect studies conducted entirely within the FVB background, the design of most FVB studies, in which a transgenic or treated group is compared with a wild-type or untreated group of the same strain.

Our within-FVB/NJ comparisons show that the strain-level bias cancels almost completely in such contrasts: the diet and treatment effects estimated under the three arms were nearly identical gene by gene (Pearson r ≥ 0.99), the imiquimod response in skin was detected with similar power under every arm, and the catalog genes did not deviate.

What the reference does change in a within-strain design is the absolute expression attributed to a catalog gene — for example the apparent level of *Rps2* or *Ndufs5* in a FVB/NJ sample — which matters when expression levels are compared across strains or across studies, when a gene is used as a normaliser, or when absolute abundance is interpreted, but not for a fold-change between two groups of the same strain.

v1_text: This note documents why that liftover step produced empty output BAMs for every dataset, explains the underlying cause, and describes the validated alternative strategy used throughout the analysis.
new_text: This note documents why that liftover step produced empty output BAMs for every dataset, explains the underlying cause, and describes the validated alternative strategy used throughout the analysis.

v1_text: Our core conclusions are primarily derived from the three substrain-matched FVB/NJ datasets (adipose, liver, kidney), in which 30 of the 32 catalog genes were confirmed.
The remaining two genes (*Fau* and *Pgam1*) were identified with support from the FVB/N cardiac dataset.
This concordance suggests that the bias is not an artifact of a single substrain, but a reproducible feature shared across the FVB lineage.
The adipose, liver, and kidney datasets therefore provide the strongest substrain-matched evidence base in our analysis.
The cardiac and PyVT datasets used FVB/N.

Although these datasets have a substrain mismatch, they provide useful external support: the FVB/NJ-derived reference still recovered substantial FVB signal at these loci, and 30 of the 32 catalog genes were independently supported by the substrain-matched datasets alone.
This suggests that the core catalog is robust and that many high-impact variants are shared between these closely related FVB substrains.
*Rsph3a* provides the clearest example.
It qualified in all three FVB/NJ-matched datasets and was also biased in the cardiac dataset.
It was not detected in the PyVT tumour dataset, so copy-number confounding was not an issue.
Rsph3a is therefore the cleanest example of a reproducibly biased FVB locus in this study.
Fau illustrates a different pattern.
It showed the largest single-tissue bias, especially in cardiac muscle.
The cardiac dataset was FVB/N rather than FVB/NJ, so the exact contribution of FVB/N-private variants cannot be fully resolved here.
Even so, correction by the FVB/NJ personalised reference was large.

This suggests, without proving, that many high-impact variants at this locus are shared between FVB/N and FVB/NJ, or that the FVB/NJ reference is sufficiently close to recover much of the lost FVB signal.
WASP partially corrected this imbalance, as expected because it removes reads whose alignment changes after allele substitution \[7\].
This result has a practical implication.
The near-zero genome-wide effect of WASP in our pure-strain comparisons reflects the sparse distribution of FVB-specific SNPs across the transcriptome, rather than algorithmic failure.
WASP produced a measurable but incomplete correction of allele balance in F1 hybrids, where reads explicitly overlap heterozygous sites (Fig. 2A).
In pure-strain analyses, however, too few reads overlapped informative SNPs to shift transcriptome-wide averages.
WASP therefore remains valuable for allele-specific analyses, while its utility for pure-strain differential expression is limited by the small fraction of informative reads.
The relevant reads may fail to align or may be assigned to another locus in a way that is not rescued by fractional multi-mapper counting.
Gm8909, Mir6236, and H2-Q5 were clear examples of this class.
For these genes, multi-mapping-inclusive counting is insufficient, and a strain-matched reference is needed to recover the FVB signal.
The adipose dataset requires a separate comment.
FVB adipose samples had a much lower uniquely mapped read fraction than B6 adipose samples under B6-reference alignment, and the difference was larger than in the other tissues.
Switching FVB reads to the FVB personalised reference recovered only part of this gap, suggesting that the adipose mapping-rate difference is not explained by SNP-mediated reference mismatch alone.
Other factors may contribute, including tissue-specific repeat content, unannotated transcripts, cell-type composition, library features, or other dataset-specific effects.
This global mapping-rate issue is separate from the locus-level bias catalog.
At catalog genes in adipose tissue, the FVB reference still recovered the expected reference-dependent signal.
The PyVT tumour dataset raised a different interpretive problem.
Fourteen catalog genes showed negative bias in PyVT despite positive mean bias across the four non-tumour tissues, and these genes were flagged as pvt_discordant.
A plausible explanation is somatic copy-number change in the tumour genome.
The MMTV-PyVT model is a widely used mammary tumour model established on the FVB/N background \[6\].
Previous genomic work has shown that PyVT mammary tumours can carry somatic copy-number alterations \[11\].
If a locus has SNP-mediated mapping bias in normal tissue but copy-number loss in the tumour, the two effects can oppose one another.
RNA-seq alone cannot distinguish these mechanisms, and matched DNA sequencing or independent copy-number calls would be needed.
For this reason, the PyVT dataset was retained as a separate annotation and was not used to define the catalog.
This caution extends beyond the PyVT model.
In tumour RNA-seq, reference bias and copy-number imbalance can interact.
A naive analysis may make reference bias appear smaller, larger, or even reversed, depending on the direction of copy-number change.
Tumour datasets therefore require extra caution.
When possible, RNA-seq interpretation should be paired with DNA-based copy-number information, especially at loci that are SNP-dense or appear in a bias catalog.
For studies focused on catalog genes, we recommend FVB/NJ personalised reference alignment when appropriate.
B6-reference assemblies in this survey included legacy mm9/mm10 as well as GRCm38/mm39/GRCm39 nomenclature when reported in GEO metadata.

v1_text: `g2gtools convert -f bam --reverse` was applied to FVB-aligned BAMs for all five datasets (three paired-end: GSE123875, GSE123893, GSE123894;
two single-end: GSE135230, GSE175625).
In every case, the converter reported 100% failure:
The representative samples above were confirmed by `samtools flagstat` to contain zero alignments in the output BAMs.
The identical failure pattern was observed in all remaining samples across all five datasets.

To confirm that quantification with the B6 GTF is equivalent to quantification with the FVB GTF for this SNP-only VCI, we compared per-gene assigned read counts from two approaches applied to the same FVB-aligned BAMs:
- **fvb_b6gtf**:

FVB-aligned BAMs × B6 Ensembl 110 GTF (used throughout the analysis)
- **fvb_fvbgtf**:
FVB-aligned BAMs × FVB/NJ GTF (Ensembl 110 converted by g2gtools)
Assigned read totals for representative datasets:
The larger difference in PE datasets reflects that the B6 GTF covers approximately 3.0% more annotated genes than the FVB GTF (57,568 vs 55,841 gene entries;
1,727 genes were not convertible by g2gtools).
With featureCounts paired-end mode (`-p`), gene coverage directly affects how many fragment pairs are assigned.
For SE datasets, gene-boundary differences have a smaller effect because single-end counting does not require both mates to fall within the same feature.

The critical validation is that per-gene *bias values* (log₂FC_fvb − log₂FC_naive) are negligibly different between the two approaches: the mean absolute bias difference across all 32 catalog genes was < 0.001 log₂ units (i.e., below the precision of the values as reported in the text and figures).

This equivalence holds because edgeR TMM normalisation adjusts for library-size differences between arms, and any systematic read-count shift from the additional B6 GTF gene coverage cancels when computing the difference between log₂FC estimates.
Genes exclusive to the B6 GTF (absent from the FVB GTF) are removed from catalog consideration by the FVB GTF presence filter described in *Methods: Bias catalog construction*.
These reads are absent from both the multi-mapper pool and the uniquely-mapped pool;
residual fractions ranged from −0.39 to 0.35).
The most extreme examples are *Gm55594* (residual = −0.08;
bias reverses sign with multi-mapping inclusion), *Tuba1b* (residual = 0.10), and *Fau* (4-tissue mean residual = 0.21;
cardiac-tissue residual = 0.15;
see below).
The clearest examples are *Gm8909* (residual = 1.00;
SNP density 75.95 SNPs/kb — the highest in the catalog;
reads simply cannot align to any locus), *Mir6236* (residual = 0.97;
a miRNA with no close paralog), and *H2-Q5* (residual = 0.85;
MHC class I gene, highly divergent sequence).
The cardiac *Fau* bias (+3.67 log₂ unique-only) shows the largest Δ among catalog genes in any single tissue: bias_multi = +0.55 log₂ (residual fraction 0.15).
This indicates that 85% of the cardiac unique-only *Fau* bias arises from SNP-induced multi-mapping rather than direct read misalignment.
*Fau* encodes a ubiquitin–40S ribosomal protein S30 fusion and belongs to a multi-copy gene family with paralogs distributed across the genome;

its 23 FVB/NJ SNPs appear to narrow the alignment score gap between the canonical *Fau* locus and related sequences, causing FVB cardiac reads to become multi-mappers in the B6 alignment while mapping uniquely to the FVB personalised reference.
Importantly, this mechanistic characterisation does not diminish the practical impact of the bias.

Investigators using standard unique-only pipelines — the default featureCounts counting mode in which multi-mapping reads are excluded — would observe the full +3.67 log₂ underestimation of FVB *Fau* expression in cardiac tissue, regardless of whether its origin is direct misalignment or SNP-induced multi-mapping.
Both mechanisms produce the same outcome under unique-only pipelines:
FVB expression is underestimated at the affected locus.

From a correction standpoint, both classes are substantially mitigated by the FVB personalised reference arm: in both cases, FVB reads align with greater specificity to the FVB-matched locus, substantially increasing recovery of the FVB read signal that is suppressed under B6-reference alignment.
